name: Harry Wetherald

education.notes: Oxford attendance reported in secondary sources (Crunchbase). Exact degree and dates not confirmed.

careerSteps.role: Product Manager → Director of Product Management
keyDecisions: Joined Tessian very early (seed stage) and led product through the scale-up to the Proofpoint acquisition in 2023
Spent the pre-LLM era training ML models to spot security incidents in email — built AI product intuition before GenAI hype
Stayed for ~10 years across startups/AI/security per his own bio — long enough to develop sharp opinions on remediation vs prioritisation
lessons: Pre-LLM era at Tessian gave a front-row view of how attackers scale tactics (phishing kits, phishing-as-a-service) once unit economics flip — instinct now central to Maze's thesis
Leading product for VM-adjacent teams is the cheapest way to find your wedge: the unmet need is in remediation, not yet another prioritisation score
Building ML products before GenAI made him allergic to over-claimed AI demos
careerSteps.notes: Part of the Tessian alumni cluster (along with Omnea's Ben Freeman and Ben Allen). Tessian was acquired by Proofpoint in 2023; Harry left in 2024 to start Maze.

keyDecisions: Spent 3-5 months on cold outreach to CISOs and security leaders before committing to the wedge: 'vulnerability's just killing us… 40% year-on-year growth in number of vulnerabilities'
Validated that the pain was remediation/triage, not prioritisation — sharpened the wedge before writing a line of product code
lessons: Cold-outreaching a few hundred buyers before building is the cheapest validation for a category-creation play
If a problem keeps coming up unprompted across 50+ CISO calls, the wedge is real
careerSteps.notes: Self-described discovery phase. Co-founders Adrian Jozwik and Santiago Castineira came from Tessian, Elastic and Amazon — design and engineering counterweights to Harry's product background.

keyDecisions: Co-founded Maze in 2024 with Adrian Jozwik (Elastic, Tessian) and Santiago Castineira (Amazon)
Bet on agentic AI for cloud vulnerability triage and remediation, not for prioritisation scoring
Started narrow on cloud CVEs (VMs, containers, infra) rather than chasing a broad 'AI for security' pitch
Raised $6M seed led by Cherry Ventures, then $25M Series A led by Theory Ventures within ~9 months — $31M total inside the first year
Came out of stealth mid-2025 with paying customers including two Fortune 200 enterprises
lessons: Treat AI agents like 'knowledgeable 16-17 year olds': they need tight tasks, guardrails and oversight — not vague open-ended prompts
In security, the right wedge is removing 90%+ of the deck of cards (false-positive vulns) rather than re-sorting them
Start at the root of the problem (is this exploitable?) before automating downstream remediation — auto-fixing 480 noise findings is worse than auto-fixing 5 real ones
Founders who lived the pain (PM/eng leads at a VM-adjacent scale-up) ship sharper wedges than outsiders
Reasoning in 5-year horizons (assume attackers scale 10-100x with AI) reframes what is 'good enough' security today
Don't try to one-for-one replace humans with AI. Instead ask: 'What would I do if my day was 100x longer?' — that's the long-tail value
careerSteps.notes: Maze deploys agents that interrogate vulnerabilities the way a senior security engineer would, at scale across millions of findings. Core insight: most vulns aren't actually exploitable in context, so the real product is intelligent triage + remediation, not another priority score.

outcomes.currentStatus: Co-founder & CEO of Maze (London). $31M raised across Seed (Cherry) and Series A (Theory) within 12 months of founding. Agents in production at 10+ orgs, including two Fortune 200 enterprises.

lessons.lesson: Founders should pick wedges where their last job gave them painful, tacit knowledge — Maze exists because Harry and his team hated VM workflows internally at Tessian.
AI agents are not autonomous senior engineers; they are knowledgeable juniors. Design products around tight, guard-railed tasks.
lessons.source: Unsupervised Learning podcast — Daniel Miessler with Harry Wetherald

lessons.lesson: Don't try to one-for-one replace humans with AI. Instead ask: 'What would I do if my day was 100x longer?' — that's the long-tail value.
lessons.source: Unsupervised Learning podcast — Daniel Miessler with Harry Wetherald

lessons.lesson: Strategic horizon-shifting: assume attackers become 10-100x more efficient with AI in 5 years and back-solve what your defences must look like today.

lessons.lesson: 3-5 months of cold-outreach to CISOs before writing code is the cheapest way to validate a category-creation play.
